title: Git Basics: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on Git: the mental model of its three areas, the core add/commit workflow, everyday inspection, branching, remotes, .gitignore and the mistakes beginners make most. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: What Git Is and the Three Areas
points: Git is a distributed version control system: every clone holds the full history, so commits, log and diff work offline
Three areas: working tree (files on disk) → staging area/index (what the next commit will contain) → repository (.git, committed history)
A commit is an immutable snapshot of the staged files with a message, author and parent pointer, identified by a SHA-1 hash
git add moves changes working tree → staging; git commit moves staging → repository; git restore moves them back
A file is untracked, modified, staged or committed; git status tells you which

chapters.title: Core Workflow: init, clone, add, commit
points: git init creates a .git folder in the current directory; git clone <url> copies the full repo and sets remote origin
git add <file> stages one file; git add . stages everything under the current directory, including new files
git commit -m "msg" records the staged snapshot; git commit -am stages tracked files only, never new files
One commit = one logical change with an imperative message such as "Fix login redirect"
git commit --amend rewrites the last commit's message or contents; use it only before pushing

chapters.title: Inspecting State: status, log, diff
points: git status shows branch, staged, unstaged and untracked files; run it before every commit
git diff compares working tree vs staging; git diff --staged compares staging vs last commit
git log --oneline --graph --all shows compact history across all branches
git log -p <file> shows the patches that changed one file; git show <hash> shows a single commit
git restore <file> discards unstaged changes (irreversible); git restore --staged <file> unstages but keeps edits

chapters.title: Branches and Merging
points: A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit; HEAD points to the branch you are on
git switch -c <name> creates and switches to a branch; git branch lists them; git branch -d <name> deletes a merged one
git merge <branch> brings that branch into the current one: fast-forward if history is linear, otherwise a merge commit
A merge conflict leaves <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers: edit the file, git add it, then git commit
Commit or stash before switching branches, or uncommitted changes may block the switch or follow you

chapters.title: Remotes, Push/Pull and .gitignore
points: A remote is a named URL (usually origin); git remote -v lists them
git push -u origin <branch> publishes a branch and sets its upstream; later plain git push works
git fetch downloads remote commits without changing your files; git pull = fetch + merge (or rebase with --rebase)
A push is rejected when the remote has commits you lack: pull first, resolve conflicts, then push; avoid git push --force on shared branches
The .gitignore file lists patterns (node_modules/, *.log, .env) so untracked files are skipped; it does not affect files already tracked: run git rm --cached <file> first
Never commit secrets: once pushed, removing the file in a later commit does not erase it from history

chapters.title: Git Basics Cheat Sheet
points: Start: git init, git clone <url>, git config --global user.name and user.email
Save: git status, git add <file>, git commit -m "msg", git diff, git diff --staged
History: git log --oneline --graph, git show <hash>, git restore <file>, git restore --staged <file>
Branches: git switch -c <name>, git merge <name>, git branch -d <name>
Remotes: git remote -v, git fetch, git pull, git push -u origin <branch>
Top mistakes: committing secrets, git add . picking up junk, force-pushing shared branches, committing on the wrong branch, forgetting git status
